newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen says it won't charge kidnappers of Poles.
newsitem.headline: Yemen says it won't charge kidnappers of Poles.

text.p: Yemen on Wednesday told the abductors of five Polish tourists that if they let the group go they would not be prosecuted for the kidnapping or the attack on security forces trying to intervene, a Polish diplomat in Sanaa said.
"The kidnappers received today a letter of guarantee from the government that they will not be punished after the release of the hostages," Stanislaw Smolen, Polish consul to Sanaa told Reuters.
"Negotiations are about to reach a successful end...Some financial conditions are still to be discussed," he added without giving details.
Yemeni officials were not immediately available for comment.

The tourists -- three men and two women between the ages of 50 and 64 -- were kidnapped on their way to archaeological sites in western Yemen last week. It was the second abduction of European holidaymakers within a month.

The tourists were abducted by members of the Al al-Masni tribe in the Khawlan area, about 65 km (40 miles) east of the capital Sanaa. Diplomats said the abduction took place sometime between Tuesday and Thursday.
On Friday, the tribesmen fired rocket-propelled grenades at military forces who had surrounded them, killing three soldiers and wounding five.
Yemeni authorities on December 19 freed five Dutch tourists who were abducted and briefly held by tribesmen while touring an area 240 km (150 miles) north of Sanaa.

In recent years, tribes in Yemen with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have kidnapped tourists or other foreigners to use as bargaining chips. The tribes' demands have usually involved land or water issues, and have rarely been political.
The current standoff is the first kidnapping involving the Al al-Masni tribe, which lives in the Beni Jabr area near Khawlan.
